doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Sitting in as a teenager; Willie Wells, the trumpeter of the century
summary: Fuller says he sat in with Frank Foster and others, and singles out Willie Wells who was Milt Jackson's friend and played a rotary-valve trumpet.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Let’s talk about you’re in high school, when do you start to hit the scene and what was your peer group when you did that in Detroit?

Well, it really wasn’t my peer group, I was way over my head. I was sitting in with Frank Foster who would be sitting in with Wardell Grey and Stony Nightingale and all those names that you probably would never hear in your life.
Well let’s put those names on the record. It’s important.

There was another guy, when Miles Davis moved to Detroit not only because of the little girl he fell in love with, Jane Peterson, but there was this trumpet player there. He was Milt Jackson’s best friend, his name was Willy Wells. That was the trumpet player of the century, for me, before Kenny Dorham. I mean, the slickness of Kenny Dorham and the technique of Freddie Hubbard. The drawback was that he played an old German rotary valve trumpet. What was it called? It’s in the trumpet family, that’s not what it’s called. You see it in Italy, it’s sort of like flugelhorn, and it had a flugel sound. He was all over that prettiness and staggering the notes, that was him. Miles took that phrase in so many directions, as Miles took some of his style from Ahmad Jamal, who is a piano player.
